questions.explain: Without a volume mount, database files live in the container's writable layer, which disappears the moment the container is removed. Named volumes persist independently of container lifecycle.
options: They are automatically copied to the image registry as a new image layer
They are migrated to the host's default data directory by Docker
They are archived to /var/opt/mssql/log on the host
They live in the container's writable layer and are lost when the container is removed
questions.q: What happens to SQL Server's database files if you run the mssql container without any volume mount and then remove the container?

questions.explain: ReadWriteOnce allows only one node to mount the volume read-write — correct for a single database instance. ReadWriteMany would let two SQL Server instances write to the same data directory simultaneously, which is corruption, not high availability.
options: ReadWriteMany, so multiple pods can share one data directory for failover
ReadWriteOnce, since only one SQL Server instance may write to a data directory at a time
ReadOnlyMany, because databases in Kubernetes never write to disk
ReadWriteOncePod, which is the only mode that supports FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING
questions.q: Which Kubernetes PVC access mode is correct for a SQL Server data directory, and why?

questions.explain: Unlike Deployments, StatefulSets give each pod a stable network identity and a persistent volume that follows it — when pod mssql-0 restarts, it gets the same PVC back, and volumeClaimTemplates create one dedicated PVC per replica.
options: StatefulSets give each pod a stable identity and a dedicated PVC that follows it across restarts and rescheduling
Deployments cannot pull the mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server image from a registry
StatefulSets automatically configure Always On AG quorum between pods
Deployments are limited to stateless images and cannot run a database process
questions.q: Why does the chapter say StatefulSets — not Deployments — are the right Kubernetes workload type for databases?

questions.explain: Major-version upgrades are operationally cleaner in containers: stop the old container, pull the new image, and start it against the same data volume — the engine upgrades the system databases automatically on first boot. Keep a tested backup from before the switch in case the upgrade fails.
options: Run ALTER DATABASE ... UPGRADE on every database before pulling the new image
Delete the data volume and restore from backup, since images cannot be upgraded in place
Stop the old container, pull the new image, and start it against the same data volume — the engine upgrades system databases on first boot
Build a new derived image with COPY mssql.conf and attach a fresh empty volume
questions.q: How does a major-version upgrade of containerized SQL Server work, according to the chapter?

questions.explain: If SQL Server sizes itself for a 256 GB host while the container is limited to 8 GB, it will meet the OOM killer. Cap the engine with MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB (or max server memory) under the container's memory limit.
options: MSSQL_PID, which limits memory to the edition's maximum
MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB (or max server memory), set below the container's memory limit
MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD, which the engine uses to derive a memory ceiling
ACCEPT_EULA=Y, which opts the container into host-memory auto-detection
questions.q: Which setting prevents SQL Server from being OOM-killed inside a memory-limited container?
